function chain()
    g = BipartiteGraph{Nothing}()
    # right 100-101-102-103-104, each step through its own left vertex
    for i in 0:3
        add_edge!(g, i + 1, 100 + i, nothing)
        add_edge!(g, i + 1, 100 + i + 1, nothing)
    end
    add_v!(g, 200)  # isolated right vertex
    return g
end

g = chain()
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 100, 2) == 0
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 2) == 2
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 2) == 3          # true length 4, capped
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 4) == 4
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 104, 4) == 5          # true length 8, capped
@assert shortest_path(g, 102, 100, 4) == 4          # symmetric
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 200, 4) == 5          # disconnected
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 999, 4) == 5          # missing
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 2.5) == 3.5
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 2.5) == 2

# epsilon 3 reaches distance 2 but not 4
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 3) == 2
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 3) == 4

d = shortest_path_metric(g, 4)
@assert d(100, 102) == 4
@assert d(102, 100) == 4   # hits the cache from the other side
@assert d(100, 104) == 5
@assert d(200, 100) == 5
@assert d(100, 100) == 0

h = map_graph(g, 2, shortest_path_metric(g, 2))
@assert num_vertices(h) == 6
@assert sort(collect(keys(h.adj))) == [100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 200]

```bash
julia --project=. -e '
include("src/map.jl")
include("src/sp.jl")

function chain()
    g = BipartiteGraph{Nothing}()
    # right 100-101-102-103-104, each step through its own left vertex
    for i in 0:3
        add_edge!(g, i + 1, 100 + i, nothing)
        add_edge!(g, i + 1, 100 + i + 1, nothing)
    end
    add_v!(g, 200)  # isolated right vertex
    return g
end

g = chain()
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 100, 2) == 0
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 2) == 2
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 2) == 3          # true length 4, capped
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 4) == 4
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 104, 4) == 5          # true length 8, capped
@assert shortest_path(g, 102, 100, 4) == 4          # symmetric
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 200, 4) == 5          # disconnected
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 999, 4) == 5          # missing
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 2.5) == 3.5
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 2.5) == 2

# epsilon 3 reaches distance 2 but not 4
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 101, 3) == 2
@assert shortest_path(g, 100, 102, 3) == 4

d = shortest_path_metric(g, 4)
@assert d(100, 102) == 4
@assert d(102, 100) == 4   # hits the cache from the other side
@assert d(100, 104) == 5
@assert d(200, 100) == 5
@assert d(100, 100) == 0

h = map_graph(g, 2, shortest_path_metric(g, 2))
@assert num_vertices(h) == 6
@assert sort(collect(keys(h.adj))) == [100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 200]
@assert !node_exists(h, 1)             # left vertices stay out
@assert num_edges(h) == 4              # consecutive pairs only
for a in 100:103
    @assert has_edge(h, a, a + 1)
    @assert edge_weight(h, a, a + 1) == 2.0
    @assert !has_edge(h, a, a)
end
@assert !has_edge(h, 100, 102)
@assert degree(h, 200) == 0

h4 = map_graph(g, 4, shortest_path_metric(g, 4))
@assert has_edge(h4, 100, 102)
@assert edge_weight(h4, 100, 102) == 4.0
@assert !has_edge(h4, 100, 104)       # length 8 > 4
@assert !has_edge(h4, 100, 200)

# frozen graph agrees
fg = freeze(g)
@assert shortest_path(fg, 100, 102, 2) == 3
@assert shortest_path(fg, 100, 102, 4) == 4
hf = map_graph(fg, 2, shortest_path_metric(fg, 2))
@assert num_vertices(hf) == num_vertices(h)
@assert num_edges(hf) == num_edges(h)
@assert edge_weight(hf, 101, 102) == 2.0

# arbitrary metric ignores edges
habs = map_graph(g, 2, (a, b) -> abs(a - b))
@assert has_edge(habs, 100, 102) && edge_weight(habs, 100, 102) == 2.0
@assert !has_edge(habs, 100, 103)
@assert has_edge(habs, 100, 200) == false

# epsilon 0 keeps vertices and drops every positive distance
h0 = map_graph(g, 0, shortest_path_metric(g, 0))
@assert num_vertices(h0) == 6
@assert num_edges(h0) == 0

@assert_throws ArgumentError shortest_path(g, 100, 101, -1)
@assert_throws ArgumentError map_graph(g, Inf, (a, b) -> 0)

# input graph is unchanged
@assert length(g.adjV) == 6
println("ok")
'
```

_**Agent (grok-4.7)**_

`src/map.jl` builds that graph, and `src/sp.jl` supplies a shortest-path distance you can pass in as the metric.

```julia
include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "src", "map.jl"))
include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "src", "sp.jl"))

h = map_graph(g, 2, shortest_path_metric(g, 2))
```

`map_graph` takes a `BipartiteGraph` or a `FrozenBipartite`, a finite `epsilon ≥ 0`, and any two-argument metric. The result is an undirected graph whose vertices are exactly the right-side vertices. Distinct vertices `r1` and `r2` are linked when `metric(r1, r2) ≤ epsilon`, and the edge weight is that distance. The metric is called once per unordered pair, smaller id first, so an embedding distance works the same way:

```julia
h = map_graph(g, 0.5, (r1, r2) -> abs(x[r1] - x[r2]))
```

`shortest_path(g, r1, r2, epsilon)` is the number of bipartite edges on a shortest path between two right-side vertices. Two items that share a neighbor are at distance 2, so with this metric an `epsilon` below 2 leaves the graph edgeless. The walk stops before the next hop would pass `epsilon`. Anything still unreached comes back as `epsilon + 1`, which fails the `≤ epsilon` test, so `map_graph` draws no edge. `shortest_path_metric(g, epsilon)` is the same rule as a metric, and it searches the ball around each source once and reuses it for the other targets. Pass it the same `epsilon` you pass to `map_graph`.

A Julia 1.12 world age issue prevents calling methods defined by `include` inside a function.

Including the files at top level is not enough. `map_dataset` was defined before the `include` statement, so its world is still older than `degree_reduce!`.

The file loads and defines `map_dataset` before the bottom block executes. Including `reduction.jl` at top level in that block still leaves `map_dataset` in an older world, so it cannot call the newer `degree_reduce!`.

The error is a classic Julia "include-from-function" problem. `map_dataset` calls `include()` internally, so the new method exists in a newer world but the caller remains in the older world and cannot invoke it.

The fix is to include `reduction.jl` and `sp.jl` at the top of the file before `map_dataset` is defined. This ensures `degree_reduce!` exists in the same world when `map_dataset` is compiled, so the main block can call it without a world age mismatch.

The top-level include fix is insufficient. The problem is calling `include()` from inside `map_dataset` itself, which defines new methods during that same function invocation. The caller remains in the older world and cannot invoke those newly defined methods.

Top-level includes before the call actually work. The main block enters `map_dataset` in the latest world, so it can invoke `degree_reduce!` even if the function was defined earlier. The restriction is only that a function cannot call methods defined after it starts executing.

The internal `include` calls inside `map_dataset` and `_ensure_map_deps` should be removed. Including `reduction.jl` and `sp.jl` unconditionally at the top of `map.jl` ensures `map_dataset` works for both direct main execution and library use. Loading `map.jl` will also pull in those dependencies.

Always including `reduction.jl` and `sp.jl` at the top of `map.jl` adds overhead for `map_graph` users, but it is correct. The three options are a top-level include in the main block only, unconditional top-level includes, or `invokelatest`, which is ugly.

Option D is to move the main script body to top level after the includes, avoiding a function defined before the include. Option A still works: top-level code calling map_dataset after the include uses the latest world age, so degree_reduce! is visible inside the function.

Unconditional top-level includes risk method overwrite warnings if `reduction.jl` is already loaded. Adding `isdefined` guards at the top level prevents duplicate includes and suppresses those warnings.

Running `src/map.jl` as the script loads the dataset you name, degree-reduces it, builds the shortest-path similarity graph, and prints how many nodes and edges are left.

```bash
julia --project=. src/map.jl konect-small/euroroad --theta=2 --epsilon=2
```

`--theta` is the degree cutoff from `reduction.jl`: vertices below that degree are removed until a sweep deletes nothing. `--max-iters=N` stops after N sweeps. `--epsilon` is the shortest-path cutoff, so two remaining right-side vertices are linked when their distance is at most that value.
